title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & IaC CI/CD ops guide (addendum)
author: Priya Nambiar
body:
Overview

Purpose: This addendum consolidates operational guidance for the GPU fleet and associated cloud accounts, networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and runbooks used by the Infra team. It is intended as a practical, hands-on reference for engineers oncall and engineers making changes to the fleet or infra automation.

Scope: GPU capacity planning, cloud account isolation and tagging, VPC/networking patterns for inference and control plane, Terraform module standards, CI/CD pipeline requirements (plan/test/apply), and concrete runbooks for common incidents.

Goals
- Keep GPU cluster availability >= 99.9% for production workloads.
- Maintain healthy utilization: target sustained utilization 60\u201370% per pool; burstable to 85% for short windows.
- Ensure Terraform modules are versioned, tested, and safe to apply in automated pipelines.
- Provide clear runbooks for common incidents: node failure, OOM, network partition, and account misconfiguration.

Ownership & Contacts
- Fleet capacity primary: infra-gpu (rotation: @gpu-oncall). Secondary: infra-sre.
- Cloud accounts, billing & quotas: cloud-accounts team.
- IaC modules & pipeline ownership: infra-iac.
- Networking & VPCs: infra-networking.
- Pager escalation matrix: see runbook references in Related pages.

High-level Architecture and Account Model
- Accounts: production (prod), staging (stg), dev (dev), sandbox (shared). Production accounts are isolated, locked-down, and have separate billing exports and KMS keys.
- VPCs: each account has a VPC-per-region. Control-plane services (autoscaler, scheduler, monitoring) run in dedicated subnets with stricter egress rules. GPU worker nodes run in worker subnets with host-based security controls.
- Network segmentation:
  - Control plane subnet: restricted inbound, only monitoring/ops ports open.
  - Worker subnet: allows outbound to model storage + control plane; limited ingress to SSH/management from bastion.

Capacity Planning (GPU Fleet)
- Target utilization: 60\u201370% steady-state. Rationale: headroom for autoscaling delays, KV cache spikes, and short bursty traffic.
- Reserve policy: keep 15\u201320% reserved capacity per pool for high-SLO customers / emergency scale-ups.
- Scale signals:
  1) Request queue length > 95th percentile threshold for 5 minutes.
  2) Average pod GPU util > 78% for 3 minutes and scheduler pending pods > 10% of pool.
  3) Model warmup latency increases and per-request tail latency (p99) breaches SLO.
- Burstback strategy: prefer adding ephemeral preemptible nodes (spot) for short bursts and only fall back to on-demand if spot capacity unavailable.
- Purchase/commit recommendations: Dedicated customers should target committed pools sized to their 95th percentile sustained QPS. Avoid provisioning >85% expected sustained utilization.

Autoscaling & Allocation Rules
- Node group sizing: prefer symmetric groups (same GPU type/family) to reduce scheduling fragmentation.
- Pod packing heuristics: scheduler bins by vGPU reservation (if enabled), memory reserve, and platform affinity.
- Eviction policy: non-critical, retriable workloads are evicted before critical SLO workloads.
- Preemption handling: when a spot node is reclaimed, drain with grace period 120s and redistribute active requests via fallback routing.

Terraform / IaC Module Guidelines
- Module naming: modules/<scope>/<purpose> (e.g. modules/gpu/node-pool).
- Semantic versioning: every module must be versioned (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and published to the internal module registry.
- Inputs & outputs: explicit, typed, and minimally permissive. Avoid passing entire objects; use primitive inputs.
- Tags & labels: all resources must include the following tags: team, env, cost_center, created_by, terraform_module.
- Testing: unit tests (terratest or kitchen-terraform) + automated plan validation must pass before merge.
- Change windows and approvals: changes affecting prod node pools or networking require a security and networking reviewer + a live runbook owner signoff.

Recommended Module Table
| Module | Responsibility | Min Required Inputs | Versioning | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| modules/gpu/node-pool | create managed node groups (GPU type, ASG settings) | gpu_type, min_size, max_size, labels | v1.2.0 | infra-iac |
| modules/network/vpc | vpc, subnet, route tables | cidr, public_subnets, private_subnets | v2.0.1 | infra-networking |
| modules/iam/service-roles | service accounts & IAM policies | team, env, services | v1.0.3 | infra-iac |

CI/CD & Build Pipelines
- Workflow stages (all PRs):
  1) Lint (terraform fmt, tflint), license header checks.
  2) Unit tests (terratest) and static checks (policy as code).
  3) terraform plan against a staging workspace. Plan outputs must be stored as pipeline artifacts for audit.
  4) Manual approval gate for prod applies if changes touch node pools, networking, IAM, or KMS.
  5) Automated apply for non-prod with branch protection rules.
- Recommended tooling: Terraform Cloud/Enterprise or Atlantis + remote state (S3/GCS with locks using DynamoDB/Firestore).
- Secrets: never store secrets in Terraform files or repo. Use encrypted secrets manager (Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault). CI agents must have ephemeral credentials and never expose long-lived keys.

Pipeline example (YAML snippet)
```
stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - plan
  - approval
  - apply

lint:
  image: hashicorp/terraform:1.4
  script:
    - terraform fmt -check
    - tflint --module

plan:
  image: hashicorp/terraform:1.4
  script:
    - terraform init -backend-config=...
    - terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - plan.tfplan
```

Runbooks (common incidents)
- Incident: Node OOM / GPU OOM (symptom: container crashes with OOM, pod restarts)
  1) Identify affected pods: kubectl get pods -o wide -n inference | grep CrashLoopBackOff
  2) Check pod logs and dmesg on node: kubectl logs <pod> && ssh node && sudo dmesg | grep -i oom
  3) If OOM is cluster-wide, scale up node pool by +1 node type-matching and cordon problematic nodes.
  4) If a single job is misbehaving, kill the pod and investigate model memory usage.
  5) Post-incident: add memory limit guardrail to the node pool module and add a monitoring rule (see Observability).

- Incident: Node failure / Node lost from ASG (symptom: node NotReady, pods pending)
  1) Check node status: kubectl describe node <node> and cloud provider instance state (gcloud/aws/ec2 describe).
  2) If instance failed, terminate and let ASG recreate. If ASG not recreating, escalate to cloud-accounts to check quotas.
  3) Re-schedule pods: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node> && verify replacement.
  4) If replacement fails due to quota, trigger capacity purchase or migrate low-priority workloads to spot.

- Incident: Networking misconfiguration (symptom: control-plane cannot reach worker metrics or model storage)
  1) Confirm connectivity: ping from control-plane to worker IPs and attempt curl to storage endpoints.
  2) Validate security groups / firewall rules and route table changes in the recent Terraform plan artifact.
  3) If the change came from a recent PR, revert plan or apply the previous plan artifact and open emergency PR.

Escalation & Communication
- Pager targets: infra-oncall -> infra-sre -> infra-eng leads -> cloud-accounts -> product-sre. Use Slack #incidents for comms, summary in the channel every 30 minutes until resolved.
- Postmortem: for Sev>=2 incidents, publish a postmortem within 48 hours in confluence under oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems. Include timeline, root cause, remediation, and action ownership.

Observability & Alerts
- Required metrics (per node & per pool): GPU_utilization, GPU_memory_used, GPU_temperature, GPU_power_draw, node_cpu_util, pod_restart_count, pod_pending_count, scheduler_pending_time.
- Dashboard suggestions: per-pool overview (utilization, avg latency p50/p95/p99, pending queue length).
- Typical thresholds:
  - GPU_utilization > 85% for 5m -> WARNING.
  - GPU_utilization > 90% for 2m -> Pager (SEV 2).
  - GPU_memory_used > 95% -> Pager (investigate OOM risk).
  - pod_pending_count > 10% of pool -> WARNING.

Change Management & Safe Deploys
1) All infra changes must be authored in a feature branch and go through CI checks.
2) For prod-impacting changes, schedule a change window and announce in #infra-changes 48h in advance.
3) Run canary apply: apply to a small staging pool, monitor for 30 minutes, then proceed to global prod apply.
4) Rollback: store plan artifacts for each apply. If an apply causes regressions, apply the previous plan artifact to revert.

Appendix: Minimal Terraform node-pool module example
```
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source  = "git::ssh://git@internal-repo/infra/modules/gpu/node-pool.git?ref=v1.2.0"
  env     = "prod"
  gpu_type = "a100-80gb"
  min_size = 4
  max_size = 40
  tags = {
    team = "infra-gpu"
    cost_center = "ML-Platform"
  }
}
```

Appendix: Quick CLI cheatsheet
- Check pod pending: kubectl get pods -n inference -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.phase=="Pending") | {name: .metadata.name, reason: .status.conditions}'
- Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
- Terraform plan in CI: terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan

Notes
- This document is intended to be actionable; if you implement changes referenced here, update the relevant modules and pipeline templates and add cross-links to the module registry.
